problems.description: app.py defines classes without PascalCase, violating the python.yaml naming pattern (one of the 3 measured convention violations).
test_notification_server.py: classes use non-PascalCase names and module-level constants are not UPPER_CASE (measured convention violations).
ClientRegistry stores connections as untyped object (dict[str, object]) rather than the concrete websocket type, weakening static guarantees across the registry API.
No authentication on the WebSocket — any connected client can emit broadcast/direct/system messages. Acceptable for session-1 greenfield per the story spec, but should be revisited in later sessions.
_new_client_id() loops with a registry lookup for a uuid4 collision that is astronomically unlikely; a plain uuid4() would suffice.

strengths: Faithful to the session-1 greenfield spec: unique client IDs, broadcast, clean disconnect handling, GET /health with connected client count, and the exact JSON message contract {type, payload, timestamp} with the required broadcast/direct/system types.
Correct tech selection per constraints: websockets library (not Flask-SocketIO) with asyncio, and a genuinely thread-safe ClientRegistry guarded by an RLock shared with the synchronous HTTP path.
Clean separation of concerns (ClientRegistry state vs NotificationServer behavior) that anticipates session 4's transport-layer extraction.
Consistent docstrings and type hints on the public surface; broadcast() gracefully prunes dead connections.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-factored, spec-compliant greenfield implementation (architectural fit 0.9) whose only real blemish is the measured convention score of 0.83 — and notably all three convention violations sit in app.py and the test file, while the main notification_server.py module itself follows PascalCase/UPPER_CASE conventions cleanly.

problems.description: New channel routing, subscribe/unsubscribe handling, and REST endpoints ship with zero test additions (AST diff +0 files); the channel-field routing logic is exactly where a bug would slip through.

Measured convention score 0.83 with 3 violations (PascalCase in app.py, test_notification_server.py; UPPER_CASE constants) — but all three are in files untouched by this diff and pre-date the commit, so the score understates this change's own conformance.
_handle_subscribe/_handle_unsubscribe duplicate the validate-channel + ack-response pattern; a shared helper would avoid the near-identical 20-line blocks.
Channel resolution is ambiguous: `message.get('channel') or payload.get('channel')` dual-sources the channel, so the effective routing key depends on caller placement of the field.
ChannelRegistry.remove_client scans every channel on disconnect (O(channels)); acceptable at this scale but linear per teardown.

strengths: ChannelRegistry mirrors the existing ClientRegistry pattern exactly (RLock + set-backed, same locking idiom), so it slots into the codebase architecture cleanly.
Dead-client cleanup was factored into _deliver and reused by both broadcast paths, removing pre-existing duplication.
Comprehensive docstring updated in lockstep with behavior (new message types, channel semantics, REST endpoints).
Empty channels are pruned on unsubscribe/disconnect, so the registry leaks no stale state.
Validation + _send_error error handling is consistent with the established _handle_direct/_handle_system flow.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, idiomatic feature addition that extends the notification server along its existing registry/handler patterns and removes duplication, though it adds no test coverage for the new routing logic.

problems.description: Abstract `broadcast` on BaseTransport (and the WebSocketTransport implementation) is dead code: the server's `_deliver` loops per-client `send_message` calls and never invokes `transport.broadcast`, leaving unused API surface on the new abstraction.

The pluggability seam is incomplete: `run()` still hardcodes `websockets.serve(self.handler, ...)`, so adding an SSE/polling/TCP transport (promised in the docstring as 'without touching the core notification logic') would require modifying the server binding code — the docstring overclaims.
No tests cover the new abstraction: `_make_transport`, the `__init_subclass__` registry, the `TRANSPORT` env var, and the unknown-transport error path (+2 classes, +1 function, +0 tests).
`NotificationServer.handler()` is now a trivial one-line delegate to `transport.on_connect`; the retained name no longer reflects its reduced responsibility.

strengths: Clean transport seam: BaseTransport ABC with `__init_subclass__`-based registry and `_make_transport` factory, mirroring the existing `broker or _make_default_broker()` dependency-injection pattern.

Core routing fully decoupled from WebSocket objects — `_handle_message`, `_handle_subscribe`, `_handle_unsubscribe`, `_handle_direct`, and `_send_error` drop the websocket parameter in favor of `client_id`.
Improved error handling in `_deliver`: dead clients detected via `send_message`'s bool return instead of silently swallowing `ConnectionClosed`.
Consistent documentation updates — module docstring, config section with `TRANSPORT` env var, and new transport-layer section all kept in sync.
Behavior-preserving, low-risk refactor confined to one source file with the default WebSocket path unchanged.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, behavior-preserving transport abstraction that follows existing DI/factory patterns and decouples routing from delivery (discrepancy note: the measured 0.83 convention score comes from pre-existing violations in app.py and test_notification_server.py, neither of which this commit touches — the diff itself is convention-clean).

problems.description: MessageStore.query() fetches the entire messages table with an unfiltered SELECT and filters channel/since in Python, so /history cost scales with total table size instead of pushing predicates into SQL (an indexed WHERE clause would keep the endpoint O(rows-matched)).

RateLimiter uses a fixed-window bucket keyed by int(time.time() // window_seconds), which allows up to 2x the limit at window boundaries rather than a true sliding window; acceptable given the Redis fallback is explicitly documented.

Mechanical scan flags 3 convention violations (PascalCase classes in app.py and test_notification_server.py; UPPER_CASE constants in test_notification_server.py) — these fall outside the primary changed file notification_server.py, whose additions (DEFAULT_* constants, class per section) are consistent with existing module style.

strengths: Cross-cutting concerns (rate limiting, message TTL, history querying) are cleanly factored into new classes and a dedicated module section banner, matching the existing Broker/MessageStore organization.
RateLimiter gracefully degrades from Redis (shared, cross-instance) to an in-memory sliding window, with RATE_LIMIT configurable via _env_int and sane defaults.
The /history endpoint returns (messages, has_more) with limit/offset pagination and robust ISO-8601 parsing (_parse_iso handles naive-UTC and trailing Z), a solid, tested public API contract.
Background TTL sweep is configurable (MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS, CLEANUP_INTERVAL_SECONDS) and started at boot, keeping history unbounded growth in check.
Added from __future__ import annotations for forward compatibility and extended the module docstring (configuration table + REST endpoints) in step with the new features.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated commit that adds rate limiting, message expiry, and a filtered history endpoint in the file's existing idioms, with only minor scalability debt (full-table scan in query, fixed-window Redis limiter) and the three flagged convention violations all outside the primary changed file.

compounding_issues: Session 1 chose a full greenfield rewrite on the `websockets` library and abandoned the provided Flask auth seed (app.py); the seed was never integrated, adapted, or deleted and sat as dead weight in the repo through all 5 sessions

Speculative cross-thread complexity from Session 1 (ClientRegistry's threading.RLock guarding a single-asyncio-loop design) persisted unchanged through Session 4's refactor, which was the natural opportunity to retire it

Measured convention violations (non-PascalCase classes, non-UPPER_CASE constants) held the convention score flat at 0.833 from Session 1 to Session 5 — flagged by analysis each session but never remediated

Session 4's transport refactor shipped with zero new tests (test count stayed at 28) and a leaky seam: WebSocketTransport reaches into server private internals (_ensure_listener, _new_client_id, _sync_channel_subscriptions), so the abstraction was never validated in isolation and future transports must know server internals

The server accreted into a single ~1165-line monolith (broker, rate limiter, stores, transport, server all in one file); Session 4 reorganized in place rather than splitting into a package, so later concerns kept inflating one module

Session 5's 'persistent message history' defaults to in-memory SQLite (`:memory:`) unless DATABASE_URL is set, and MessageStore.query/purge_older_than fetch all rows and filter/sort in Python — persistence is opt-in and history lookup does not scale
key_decisions: Discarding the unrelated Flask auth seed and building a greenfield asyncio WebSocket server on the `websockets` library — a consequential call that defined the entire architecture and test strategy from Session 1
Centralizing the canonical message contract in make_message() (validated types, payload dict, auto-timestamp), which every message type and REST path conformed to throughout the story

Constructor-injected state-holder classes (ClientRegistry, ChannelRegistry in S1-S2) established a DI pattern consistently extended to Broker, MessageStore, ConnectionStore, RateLimiter, and BaseTransport — the load-bearing architectural convention

Choosing Redis pub/sub as the message backbone with graceful degradation to in-process delivery when Redis is absent (S3), enabling multi-instance scaling while keeping the test suite green without a broker
Adding SQLite message persistence in S3, which S5's cross-cutting work naturally reused for both the /history endpoint and the TTL purge (purge_older_than)
Extracting a pluggable transport layer in S4 via a BaseTransport ABC with a __init_subclass__ factory registry and TRANSPORT env selection, anticipating SSE/polling/raw-TCP transports
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality was high from the first commit and the arc is accretive with one risk plateau: Session 1 delivered a well-factored, spec-compliant greenfield with a clean DI pattern and 10 passing tests; Session 2 added channel subscriptions cleanly (19 tests); Session 3 was the largest integration (Redis backbone + SQLite persistence, the bulk of the story's token spend) and added real complexity but stayed well-structured (28 tests); Session 4 plateaued — a large transport abstraction shipped with zero new tests and a leaky seam into server internals while the file grew into a monolith; Session 5 recovered strongly with 18 new tests (46 total, all green) for rate limiting, message expiry, and history. Net: quality improved in coverage and feature depth while the measured convention score stayed flat at 0.833, and structural cleanliness declined slightly as every concern accrued into one file.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, test-disciplined five-session build that follows a textbook greenfield-to-cross-cutting arc with strong DI and reuse (S3's store powering S5's history), let down only by an untested Session-4 abstraction, an abandoned seed codebase, and convention debt that was flagged but never paid down.
